narrative_summary.historical_use: Peppermint oil has a documented European history of digestive use; traditional cough, muscle-pain and itching applications have a separate evidence basis from oral IBS research [5].
narrative_summary.modern_application: Draft research profile: enteric-coated peppermint oil has been studied for IBS symptoms, with inconsistent trial results [1][2]. A 2022 synthesis of 10 RCTs (1030 participants) reported pooled symptom benefit but rated certainty very low and found more adverse events [1]. A 6-week trial in people with Rome IV IBS found no superiority over placebo [2]. A 2026 trial in children aged 8–18 years likewise found neither peppermint oil nor peppermint sweets superior to placebo after eight weeks [6]. BMS Level U for a firm general efficacy conclusion; formulation-specific human research exists. Pediatric PK studies describe exposure, not established pediatric treatment regimens [3][4]. Pending manual scientific review.
narrative_summary.side_effects: Heartburn, nausea and perianal burning are reported; reflux can worsen, including in people with hiatal hernia. Allergy can occur. Trial adverse events were more frequent than placebo in the synthesis [1][5].
narrative_summary.contraindications: EMA lists oil/menthol hypersensitivity, liver disease, cholangitis, gallstones, other biliary disorders and achlorhydria for oral gastro-resistant preparations. Oral IBS preparations are not recommended below age 8; other routes have distinct age restrictions, including contraindication below age 2 [5]. Worsening symptoms warrant medical advice [5]. EMA also contraindicates its traditional-use preparations in children with a seizure history; age limits vary by route [5].

clinical_data.used_part: Peppermint essential oil; clinical evidence here concerns enteric-coated oil, not leaf tea [2][5].
clinical_data.mechanism_of_action: EMA describes gastrointestinal smooth-muscle spasmolysis in human pharmacological studies. This does not establish symptom benefit in every IBS population or identify a single clinically validated molecular target [5].

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Human studies measured systemic menthol after enteric-coated oil; exposure depends on dose/formulation. In a small pediatric study peak concentration occurred about 2.5 hours after dosing [4].
pharmacokinetics.distribution: Human whole-oil tissue distribution is insufficiently characterized in the retrieved sources; pediatric PK findings do not establish adult distribution [3][4].
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: EMA describes glucuronide formation and limited clinical observations of CYP3A4 inhibition; interaction magnitude remains incompletely defined [5].
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Menthol glucuronide elimination is described in EMA; modified release delays urinary excretion relative to immediate release. No universal whole-oil half-life is established here [5].

safety_and_interactions.drug_interactions: Antacids, H2 blockers and proton-pump inhibitors may cause premature dissolution of gastro-resistant coatings. Limited CYP3A4 observations do not establish a quantified interaction with every substrate [5].
safety_and_interactions.toxicity: Concentrated oil overdose can cause serious neurologic and cardiac effects. Animal high-dose pulegone/menthofuran findings are not direct estimates of clinical cancer risk [5].

special_precautions.pregnancy: Medicinal-oil pregnancy safety is unestablished; EMA does not recommend use with insufficient data [5].
special_precautions.lactation: EMA does not recommend medicinal use; milk transfer is unknown [5].
special_precautions.hepatic_impairment: Oral gastro-resistant oil is contraindicated in liver disease in the EMA monograph [5].
special_precautions.renal_impairment: No validated renal dose adjustment identified; renal-impairment PK and safety remain gaps in this extraction [3][4][5].

narrative_summary.historical_use: Artichoke leaf has documented traditional use for fullness, bloating and flatulence; EMA categorizes this digestive indication as traditional use [4].
narrative_summary.modern_application: Draft research profile: artichoke leaf extracts have been investigated for functional dyspepsia and lipid biomarkers [1][2][3]. In a 6-week RCT (247 enrolled), a commercial leaf extract improved symptom scores versus placebo [1]. Meta-analyses reported lipid changes across varying products; cardiovascular event prevention is unproven [2][3]. BMS Level B provisional for the specific dyspepsia preparation and lipid markers, with full-text bias review pending; EMA traditional-use status remains distinct [4]. Pending manual scientific review.
narrative_summary.side_effects: Mild diarrhea, abdominal spasm, nausea, heartburn and allergic reactions are reported; frequencies are unknown [4].
narrative_summary.contraindications: EMA lists Asteraceae hypersensitivity, bile-duct obstruction, cholangitis, liver disease, gallstones and other biliary disorders requiring medical advice. Use below age 12 is not established [4]. Persistent digestive symptoms beyond two weeks warrant medical advice [4].

clinical_data.used_part: Leaf extract of cultivated artichoke, reported in literature as Cynara scolymus; evidence must not be transferred to all C. cardunculus varieties or edible hearts. EMA covers specified leaf preparations [1][4].
primary_active_compounds: Commercial leaf-extract mixture; the retrieved trial abstract does not identify constituent concentrations or clinical standardization, so no individual active compound is assigned [1].
clinical_data.mechanism_of_action: Digestive symptom modulation and lipid metabolism are studied outcomes; molecular causation is not established by the retrieved human trials. No specific molecular target is assigned here [1][2][3].

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Human absorption of the trial extract is not characterized in the retrieved studies; no bioavailability estimate assigned [1][4].
pharmacokinetics.distribution: Human tissue distribution is not characterized in the retrieved sources [1][4].
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Human metabolism of the whole leaf extract is not characterized in this extraction; no CYP claim assigned [4].
pharmacokinetics.excretion: No human elimination route or half-life established for the whole extract in the retrieved sources [4].

safety_and_interactions.drug_interactions: EMA reports no interactions; formal interaction data remain limited. This does not establish compatibility with all medicines [4].
safety_and_interactions.toxicity: Long-term human toxicity is not established by short trials. EMA notes inadequate reproductive, genotoxicity and carcinogenicity testing; no quantified human safe maximum is assigned [1][4].

special_precautions.pregnancy: Safety unestablished; EMA does not recommend medicinal use during pregnancy [4].
special_precautions.lactation: Safety unestablished; EMA does not recommend medicinal use during lactation [4].
special_precautions.hepatic_impairment: Liver disease and biliary disease are listed contraindications in EMA; experimental liver research does not override this [4].
special_precautions.renal_impairment: No renal dose-adjustment evidence identified; renal-impairment safety remains insufficiently characterized [4].

narrative_summary.historical_use: Senna leaf has longstanding laxative use; EMA recognizes well-established short-term use for occasional constipation [4].
narrative_summary.modern_application: Draft research profile: senna preparations have been studied for constipation, with short-term symptom benefits and important electrolyte and obstruction precautions [1][4]. A 28-day randomized trial in 90 adults compared senna, magnesium oxide and placebo; improvement favored active groups [1]. Exact senna part and anthranoid standardization were not specified in its abstract, so no product-specific dose is given here. BMS Level B provisional for constipation; a favorable OTC systematic review uses a different grading system [2]. EMA limits unsupervised leaf-medicine use to one week; the research duration is not general-use guidance [4]. Pending manual scientific review.
narrative_summary.side_effects: Abdominal cramps, diarrhea and allergic reactions can occur. Prolonged use may disturb fluid/electrolyte balance and cause reversible intestinal pigmentation; incidence is not established here [4].
narrative_summary.contraindications: EMA contraindications include hypersensitivity, bowel obstruction/stenosis, atony, appendicitis, inflammatory bowel disease, unexplained abdominal pain, severe dehydration, pregnancy, lactation and age under 12. Persistent constipation or symptoms suggesting obstruction require medical assessment [4].

clinical_data.used_part: EMA profile concerns senna leaf. Pods have related but separately specified preparations. Constipation RCT abstract does not identify plant part or sennoside content [1][4].
primary_active_compounds: Sennosides (hydroxyanthracene glycosides); preparations are standardized, but the RCT abstract omits content [1][4]
clinical_data.mechanism_of_action: Colonic bacteria convert sennosides to rhein anthrone; anthranoid laxative action alters colonic motility and water/electrolyte transport. Mechanism does not justify chronic unrestricted use [4].

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Sennosides are not absorbed or split by human enzymes in the upper gut; some metabolites are absorbed after colonic activation [4].
pharmacokinetics.distribution: Whole-preparation distribution is incompletely defined. EMA describes a small human pod-powder PK study; pod findings are not identical to a leaf-product PK profile [4].
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Bacterial conversion to rhein anthrone occurs in the colon; circulating metabolites include conjugates [4].
pharmacokinetics.excretion: EMA describes mainly fecal elimination with some urinary/biliary metabolite elimination; no universal leaf-extract half-life is established here [4].

safety_and_interactions.drug_interactions: Potassium depletion during prolonged misuse can potentiate cardiac glycosides and interact with antiarrhythmics; diuretics, corticosteroids and liquorice may increase potassium loss [4]. EMA advises medical consultation with QT-prolonging medicines and these interacting drug classes [4].
safety_and_interactions.toxicity: Fluid/electrolyte depletion is a principal misuse risk. A case report linked chronic senna exposure with cholestatic hepatitis, with confounders and no incidence estimate [3][4].

special_precautions.pregnancy: Contraindicated in the EMA senna-leaf monograph; experimental anthranoid findings underpin precaution [4].
special_precautions.lactation: Contraindicated by EMA; small quantities of active metabolites can enter milk [4].
special_precautions.hepatic_impairment: Suspected liver injury has been reported; no validated hepatic dose adjustment identified [3][4].
special_precautions.renal_impairment: Kidney disorders increase concern about electrolyte disturbances; no validated renal dose adjustment identified [4].

narrative_summary.historical_use: Ispaghula seed husk has established medicinal use as a bulk-forming laxative; this profile concerns husk, not unrelated Plantago species [4].
narrative_summary.modern_application: Draft research profile: psyllium husk has been studied for constipation, IBS symptoms and lipid biomarkers [1][2][3]. A 12-week IBS RCT compared psyllium, bran and placebo in 275 adults; psyllium improved relief in early months [1]. Fiber meta-analysis supports a psyllium signal but pooled all-fiber effects cannot be assigned wholly to psyllium [2]. A 28-trial lipid meta-analysis found lower LDL, with moderate certainty limited by inconsistency [3]. BMS Level B provisional for these specific outcomes pending full-text appraisal; cardiovascular event prevention is not established. Pending manual scientific review.
narrative_summary.side_effects: Flatulence, distension and allergy, including anaphylaxis, can occur. Inadequate fluid can cause choking or esophageal/intestinal obstruction; powder inhalation may sensitize [4].
narrative_summary.contraindications: EMA contraindications include swallowing/throat disorders, GI narrowing, potential/existing obstruction, megacolon, undiagnosed rectal bleeding, persistent sudden bowel-habit change and failure to defecate after a laxative. Allergy is a contraindication [4]. Constipation persisting beyond three days or abdominal pain warrants medical advice; pediatric age restrictions depend on the indication [4].

clinical_data.used_part: Seed coats (ispaghula/psyllium husk), whole or powdered. Seed, husk and other Plantago species are not interchangeable [4].
primary_active_compounds: Gel-forming mucilage polysaccharides, including arabinoxylan-type fiber; whole husk is not a purified systemic drug [4]
clinical_data.mechanism_of_action: Water-retaining mucilage increases stool hydration/bulk; predominantly local gut action differs from systemic receptor pharmacology. Lipid-marker effects do not demonstrate prevention of cardiovascular events [3][4].

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Husk mucilage is minimally absorbed intact; EMA distinguishes local fiber action from uptake of degradation products [4].
pharmacokinetics.distribution: No conventional whole-husk systemic tissue-distribution profile is established; local luminal action predominates [4].
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Limited colonic fermentation produces short-chain fatty acids; do not treat fiber as a CYP-metabolized small-molecule drug [4].
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Unabsorbed fiber and metabolites pass in feces; a conventional whole-husk elimination half-life is not applicable [4].

safety_and_interactions.drug_interactions: May delay absorption of other oral medicines. EMA specifies separation and notes supervision with thyroid hormones or motility-inhibiting drugs; diabetes therapy may require review. Interaction severity depends on the medicine [4].
safety_and_interactions.toxicity: The major acute risks are mechanical obstruction and severe hypersensitivity; sufficient liquid is essential. No maximum safe dose for impaired populations is inferred from trials [4].

special_precautions.pregnancy: EMA permits consideration when diet change fails, with limited pregnancy data; no claim of established fetal safety [4].
special_precautions.lactation: EMA allows consideration when needed; specific infant-safety evidence remains limited [4].
special_precautions.hepatic_impairment: No hepatic dose-adjustment evidence identified for husk; impairment-specific safety is not established by these trials [4].
special_precautions.renal_impairment: Fluid restrictions and swallowing/obstruction risk require individual clinical assessment; no renal dose-adjustment evidence identified [4].

narrative_summary.historical_use: Aloe has documented historical skin and wound use in several ancient medical traditions. Historical use is not evidence that contemporary gel, latex and whole-leaf products have equivalent effects [4].
narrative_summary.modern_application: Draft research profile: aloe gel preparations have been investigated for wounds and oral inflammatory-bowel symptoms, with substantial uncertainty and product differences [1][2][5]. A small 4-week UC trial (44 evaluable participants) found more clinical responses with oral gel than placebo, but clinical remission and sigmoidoscopic findings were not convincingly different [1]. The 2012 wound review found insufficient high-quality evidence [2]. A later review of nine burn RCTs reported shorter healing with aloe preparations, while pain and infection differences were not significant; these burn findings cannot be generalized to all wounds or products [5]. BMS Level C for the exploratory UC signal, provisional B for the narrower burn-healing outcome pending full-text quality appraisal, and U for a firm broad wound-healing conclusion. Gel findings do not support oral latex or whole-leaf products. Pending manual scientific review.
narrative_summary.side_effects: Topical gel may cause burning, itching or rash. Oral latex causes cramps and diarrhea. Acute hepatitis has been associated with oral aloe preparations, whose exact plant fraction may be unclear [3][4].
narrative_summary.contraindications: Known aloe hypersensitivity precludes the relevant product. Oral aloe is discouraged in pregnancy and lactation. Gel research must not be generalized to anthranoid-containing latex/whole-leaf laxatives; obstruction or unexplained abdominal symptoms require clinical assessment, not self-treatment [4].

clinical_data.used_part: Inner-leaf gel in the UC trial and varied topical products in wound research. Latex is the outer-leaf exudate; whole-leaf extracts contain different fractions and require separate safety assessment [1][2][4].
primary_active_compounds: Inner-leaf gel is a complex preparation; its clinical constituent standardization is not established in the retrieved trial abstract [1].
Aloin is an anthraquinone constituent relevant to oral aloe-product safety; gel, latex and whole-leaf extracts require separate assessment [4].
clinical_data.mechanism_of_action: Inflammatory activity was assessed clinically/histologically in the small gel trial; it does not establish a molecular mechanism. No specific receptor or signaling target is attributed from these clinical sources [1].

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Human absorption/bioavailability of the studied whole gel is not characterized in retrieved sources; no intact-polysaccharide systemic exposure assumed [1][4].
pharmacokinetics.distribution: Human tissue distribution of the gel preparation is unknown in this extraction [1][4].
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Human gel-product metabolic pathways are insufficiently characterized; anthranoid pharmacology cannot be assigned to anthranoid-depleted gel [4].
pharmacokinetics.excretion: No validated gel-product elimination route or half-life identified in the retrieved literature [1][4].

safety_and_interactions.drug_interactions: NCCIH flags increased cardiac-glycoside adverse-effect risk with latex overuse. This is preparation specific and must not be automatically assigned to topical inner-leaf gel [4].
safety_and_interactions.toxicity: Oral aloe preparations have been associated with hepatitis [3]. Non-decolorized whole-leaf extracts produced GI tumors in rodents; this is animal evidence and not interchangeable with inner gel or a quantified human cancer risk [4].

special_precautions.pregnancy: Oral gel, latex and whole-leaf products may be unsafe during pregnancy per NCCIH; topical pregnancy evidence is insufficiently characterized here [4].
special_precautions.lactation: Oral aloe may be unsafe while breastfeeding; infant exposure for specific products is inadequately characterized [4].
special_precautions.hepatic_impairment: Hepatitis reports warrant particular caution with oral products; no validated hepatic adjustment exists in these sources [3][4].
special_precautions.renal_impairment: Renal-impairment safety is inadequately characterized in the selected sources. Diarrhea-producing oral products warrant particular caution because of fluid losses; this is a precautionary inference, not a tested renal dosing rule [4].
